explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The writer says it is hard to explain “…because you are dull of hearing.” He doesn't blame the roads or the schedule. He names the problem right to their faces, and I think that took some nerve.
Nobody pulls out a map in this verse, friend. The writer never mentions distance. He says it is hard to explain “…because you are dull of hearing.” That's the whole reason he gives.

Fear is a fair guess, but the text doesn't go there. The writer says it is hard to explain “…because you are dull of hearing.” He's talking about how they listen, not what they're scared of. So the problem is their ears, baker, not their nerves.

Teachers, baker! The writer says that by this time they ought to be teachers. Instead they need someone to reteach them the basic principles of God's word. That's like a cookie shop where the head baker still needs the oven explained to him. I would know, I've had my share of oven confusion.

Prophets is a big jump, friend. The writer never says they ought to be prophets. He says they ought to be teachers by this time. Then he points out they need someone to reteach them the basic principles of God's word.

Leaders sounds close, and it's a good word. But the writer picks a different one: by this time they ought to be teachers. He follows it with a sting, that they need someone to reteach them the basic principles of God's word. So it's teachers, baker.
Close, baker, but it's the other way around. The writer says to these readers, “You need milk, not solid food!” So he's telling them they aren't ready for solid food yet. Milk first, steak later.

False is right, baker. The writer says plainly, “You need milk, not solid food!” He says it right after telling them they need someone to reteach them the basics. He's not insulting the milk, though. He's telling them where they are.

An infant, baker. The writer says everyone who lives on milk is still an infant, inexperienced in the message of righteousness. Babies drink milk and nobody laughs at them. The trouble starts when a grown adult is still ordering from the baby menu.
A traveler sounds like someone packing light, friend. But the writer's picture has no traveler in it. He says everyone who lives on milk is still an infant. Infants are the ones on milk.

A servant is a thoughtful guess, but the writer doesn't use one here. He says everyone who lives on milk is still an infant, inexperienced in the message of righteousness. It's a picture of someone who hasn't grown up yet, baker.

Good from evil, baker. The writer says the mature “by constant use have trained their senses to distinguish good from evil.” It's practice that does it, not a one-time lesson. Like me with a hot pan: first time, OUCH, and now I can feel one coming from across the kitchen.
Friend from foe is a good skill to have, friend. But the writer names something else. The mature have trained their senses “to distinguish good from evil.” That's what constant use is for here.

Old from new would help in a fridge, baker, but that's not this verse. The writer says the mature “by constant use have trained their senses to distinguish good from evil.” It's about good and evil, and the training comes from practice.

True, baker. The writer lists “repentance from dead works, and of faith in God” as part of the foundation (Hebrews 6:1). Faith in God sits right there in that first layer. Foundations aren't flashy, but nothing stands without one.

It's actually in the list, friend. The writer names “…repentance from dead works, and of faith in God” as part of the foundation. So faith in God is right there at the start. It's easy to skip past when you're looking for the big words.

If God permits, baker. The writer says, “And this we will do, if God permits.” He's not saying it with a shrug. I think he's saying the going on depends on God, not on how fired up they feel. A good baker still checks with the One who owns the kitchen.
A vote sounds tidy, friend, but the writer never mentions one. He says, “And this we will do, if God permits.” The condition is God, not a committee. No meeting needed.
That's what I'd say about my laundry, baker. But here the writer says, “And this we will do, if God permits.” The clock isn't the condition. God is.

explanations.answer: They crucify the Son of God all over again
explanations.explanation: That's what the writer says, baker. These people are “crucifying the Son of God all over again and subjecting Him to open shame.” Those are heavy words, and I think they ought to feel heavy. I won't joke on this one.

explanations.answer: They forget the words of the prophets again
explanations.explanation: The prophets don't show up in this reason, friend. The writer says it's because “they themselves are crucifying the Son of God all over again and subjecting Him to open shame.” That's the reason he gives. I think this is a heavy one to sit with.

explanations.answer: They bow down to idols of stone again
explanations.explanation: Idols are a big deal elsewhere in the Bible, baker, but they aren't in this verse. The writer's reason is that they are “crucifying the Son of God all over again and subjecting Him to open shame.” That's the reason he gives. It's a heavy part of the passage.

True, baker. The writer says land that drinks in the rain often falling on it and produces a crop useful to those for whom it is tended “receives the blessing of God.” It's a simple picture. Rain comes down, a useful crop comes up, and the blessing is there.

Flip that one, friend. The writer says land that drinks in the rain often falling on it and produces a useful crop “receives the blessing of God.” So the good land is the blessed land. It's a picture of a field doing what a field is for.

Burned, baker. The writer says the land that produces thorns and thistles is worthless, and its curse is imminent. Then he adds, “In the end it will be burned.” It's a stern picture, and the writer means it to be.

Rain shows up in the good land's picture, friend, so I see how water got in your head. But for the thorny land, the writer says, “In the end it will be burned.” No flood in this one. It's a stern picture.
Nobody's bidding on thorns, baker. The writer says land that produces thorns and thistles is worthless. Then he says, “In the end it will be burned.” There's no sale in the picture.

Salvation, baker. The writer says he is convinced of “better things in your case—things that accompany salvation.” After the heavy part, that's a deep breath of good news. He calls them beloved right before he says it.

Repentance did show up a few verses back, friend, so I get the mix-up. But here the writer says he is convinced of better things in their case, “things that accompany salvation.” That's the word he lands on.

Obedience is a good word, baker, but it's not the one in this verse. The writer says he is convinced of better things in their case, “things that accompany salvation.” That's the word that fits the blank.
Work, baker. The writer says, “For God is not unjust. He will not forget your work and the love you have shown for His name…” That's good news for anybody who's kept showing up. God sees every batch.

Wealth is not what he says, friend. The writer says, “He will not forget your work and the love you have shown for His name…” It's their work that counts here, not their bank account. I'm a stamper who started out as a 25 cent price tag, so that sounds just right to me.

Words are easy to give, baker, and the writer picks something else. He says, “He will not forget your work and the love you have shown for His name…” It's their work and their love for His name that he points to.

It's the other way around, baker. The writer says God will not forget their work and the love they've shown for His name “…as you have ministered to the saints and continue to do so.” So they haven't stopped. They're still at it.
False, baker. The writer says they have ministered to the saints “and continue to do so.” Notice that second part, because it means they're still going. That's a nice thing to hear after the thorns.

Diligence, baker. The writer says, “We want each of you to show this same diligence to the very end, in order to make your hope sure.” Diligence just means keeping at it. Like a timer that keeps ticking until the batch is done.

Caution is a good habit near a hot oven, friend, but it's not the word here. The writer wants each of them to show “this same diligence to the very end.” He's asking them to keep at it, not to tiptoe.

Sorrow would be a gloomy ending, baker, and that's not where the writer goes. He says, “We want each of you to show this same diligence to the very end, in order to make your hope sure.” Diligence is the word. He means keep at it.

Faith and patience, baker. The writer says they will imitate those who “through faith and patience inherit what has been promised.” Faith trusts, and patience waits. Waiting on a batch is easy compared to that.
Prayer and fasting are good things, friend, but they aren't the pair in this verse. The writer says those people inherit what has been promised “through faith and patience.” That's the pair he names.
Those two sound like a strong team, baker, and the writer chose a different pair. He says those who inherit what has been promised do it “through faith and patience.” Those are the two to remember.
